host_timing_note: Measured on the FreeRTOS POSIX port, where every task is a thread of a Linux process. Times, jitter and latencies are those of the host's scheduler and are not what the same code shows on a microcontroller. The contents, orderings and sizes of protocol data, and the frames and bytes an exchange takes, do not depend on the host. What happens in a stretch of time does: the jobs and frames of a run of fixed length, ticks dropped, jobs released early; and a stall of the host past the node's 500 ms watchdog or a 1 s protocol timer fails what the node would have passed. Such a failure is never hidden (the bench counts and keeps it, or writes no result), and no stall makes a check pass, so a count of 0 failures holds whatever the host did. The trace's and the observer's times are CLOCK_MONOTONIC of the same Linux VM; a task's release, start and running time are the kernel's decisions inside vTaskSwitchContext() and the tick handler, which on this port run in host threads: the figures include the host's delivery of the tick and of thread wake-ups. The execution times and CPU shares are x86-64 times of a host thread and say nothing about a Cortex-M3; the stack depths are those of host threads with x86-64 frames. Which frame carries which sample does not depend on the host; the counts of a run do: its jobs and frames, the publishes missing on the bus, the ticks dropped and the jobs released early are what the host let the node do in the run's duration, and the result keeps every one.

tick_lead.stretch: consecutive counts each first seen before its tick was due, from the first sight of the first to the due time of the last; the trace sees the count only at a SWITCH or READY event, so a stretch begins at a sight, which can be after the count got ahead

sensor.arrival: its period's tick, as due on the base in force for that tick

health.arrival: its period's tick, as due on the base in force for that tick

process.arrival: the arrival of the sensor job whose sample released it
